summary: This standards-track document specifies the IDLE command for IMAP4, which lets a client tell the server it is ready to receive real-time updates, such as new mail, without polling.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of asking the mail server again and again whether anything changed, a client sends IDLE and waits. The server then speaks up by itself when new mail arrives, and the client says DONE when it wants to talk again.

questions: how to get push email with imap
how often should an imap client re-issue idle
subtitle: A command that lets an IMAP client wait while the server pushes mailbox updates in real time.

tldr.problem: IMAP4 requires a client to poll the server for changes to the selected mailbox, so a user does not see new mail immediately unless the client polls very often.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends IDLE, the server answers with a continuation request, and while IDLE is active the server may send untagged EXISTS, EXPUNGE and other messages at any time. The client ends it by sending DONE.
tldr.outcome: A client sees mailbox changes right away and still needs to re-issue IDLE only about every 29 minutes to avoid being logged off.

today: RFC 2177 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of the IMAP IDLE command.

sections.title: Why IMAP Clients Had to Poll
sections.content:
The base IMAP4 protocol (RFC 2060) requires a client to poll the server for changes to the selected mailbox, such as new mail or deletions. Users would rather see new mail immediately, and real-time applications built on IMAP might otherwise need to poll every few seconds.

The RFC notes that the base specification does allow a server to push EXISTS responses asynchronously, but a client cannot expect that behaviour and must poll. The IDLE command lets a client tell the server that it is ready to accept such real-time updates.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking the mail server over and over whether anything is new is wasteful and slow to notice changes. IDLE lets the client say once that it is listening and then wait quietly.

sections.title: How IDLE Works
sections.content:
IDLE takes no arguments. A client may use it only if the server lists IDLE in its CAPABILITY response; if the server does not advertise it, the client MUST NOT use IDLE and must poll. The server answers with a continuation (+) response, and from then on it is free to send untagged EXISTS, EXPUNGE and other messages at any time.

The client ends the command by sending the continuation data DONE, which satisfies the server's continuation request. The server MAY send any queued untagged responses and then MUST immediately send the tagged response to IDLE and be ready for other commands. The client MUST NOT send any other command while the server is waiting for DONE, because the server could not tell a command from a continuation. The possible results are OK after DONE, NO when the server will not allow IDLE now, and BAD.
sections.plainLanguage: You may only use the command if the server offers it. Once you send it, the server may tell you about changes whenever it likes, and it can only tell your command apart from the word DONE, so you must not type anything else until you send DONE.

sections.title: Timeouts and the 29-Minute Rule
sections.content:
A server MAY consider a client that has an IDLE command running to be inactive, and if it has an inactivity timeout it MAY log the client off at the end of that period. Because of that, clients using IDLE are advised to terminate it and re-issue it at least every 29 minutes.

This still lets a client receive immediate mailbox updates even though it only needs to check in at half-hour intervals.
sections.plainLanguage: A server may drop a silent client. To stay connected, a client should quiet-and-wait again at least every 29 minutes, which is far less often than polling every few seconds.

sections.title: Example Session and Syntax
sections.content:
The RFC's example selects INBOX, issues A002 IDLE, and gets a + idling continuation response. New mail arrives as an untagged EXISTS response for message 4, then the client sends DONE and the server replies A002 OK IDLE terminated. Later, an untagged EXPUNGE response for message 2, caused by another client's deletion, arrives the same way while the client is idling again.

The formal syntax adds idle to the commands valid in the Authenticated or Selected state, defined simply as "IDLE" CRLF "DONE". The RFC says there are no known security issues with this extension.
sections.plainLanguage: The example shows the server announcing new mail and a deletion all by itself while the client waits, then the client saying DONE to end the wait.

references.text: Crispin, M., "Internet Message Access Protocol - Version 4rev1", RFC 2060, December 1996.
